title: INSERT and add Data - Travel Tracker Part 2
summary: Teaches INSERT INTO in SQL and parameterised queries with $1 placeholders in node-postgres, creates and imports a countries lookup table, and builds the POST /add route that converts a typed country name to its code and saves it.

concepts.heading: INSERT INTO in SQL
points: Form: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2, col3) VALUES (v1, v2, v3);
The column list order must match the order of the values. Leave out the id column so SERIAL generates it.
String values use single quotes; numbers are bare. End with a semicolon.
Exercise: insert a new world_food row for Italy with rice 1.46 and wheat 7.3, then view all rows to confirm it appears as row 10.
Inserting through SQL (rather than the pgAdmin grid) is what the app will need, because new data arrives from users at runtime.

concepts.heading: The countries lookup table
points: Users type a country name, not a two-letter code, so the backend needs a name-to-code mapping. The countries table provides it (e.g. Angola maps to AO).
Columns: id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, country_code CHAR(2), country_name VARCHAR(100). 100 characters leaves room for long official names.
Create it in the world database, then import countries.csv via Import/Export Data with Header on. This CSV already contains ids, so import all three columns.
The result is a list of every country with its ISO code.

concepts.heading: Parameterised queries in node-postgres
points: db.query(text, values) takes two arguments: the SQL string and an array of values.
In the SQL text use numbered placeholders $1, $2, $3. Each is replaced by the array item in that position.
This lets you pass variables or computed expressions (even 5*6) rather than hard-coded literals.
(Extra) Because values are sent separately from the SQL, this also prevents SQL injection, so never build the query by concatenating user input into the string.

concepts.heading: POST /add solution
points: The form in index.ejs posts to /add, so add app.post('/add', ...). body-parser is already set up, so the typed value is available as req.body['country'] (the input's name attribute is country).
First query: SELECT country_code FROM countries WHERE country_name = $1 with [input].
result.rows is an array. If it is empty the name had no match; if rows.length !== 0, take rows[0].country_code.
Second query: INSERT INTO visited_countries (country_code) VALUES ($1) with [countryCode].
Finish with res.redirect('/') so the home route re-queries and re-renders the map and total.
The visited-countries query is moved into a helper function (checkVisisted in the reference) returning the array of codes; this is optional but sets up reuse later.
Debug by console.log of result and result.rows to check the data's shape rather than hunting documentation.
Matching is exact on country_name, so entries must be spelled as in the table (Germany, Colombia work).
(Extra) The reference solution does nothing when there is no match, so the request hangs with no response. Part 3 addresses error handling.

task.name: Travel Tracker Part 2: add a country from the form
task.starting_point: Part 1 app, countries.csv in the lesson resources, and solution2.js for comparison.
task.goal: Typing a country name in the form and pressing Add saves its code to visited_countries and the map shades it with an updated total.
steps: Insert the Italy row into world_food using SQL.
Create the countries table and import countries.csv with all columns.
Check index.ejs: the form posts to /add and the input is named country.
Add an app.post('/add') route that reads req.body.country.
Look up the code in countries with a $1 placeholder.
If a row is found, INSERT the code into visited_countries.
Redirect to / so the map refreshes.
Test with names like Japan, Germany, Colombia.
task.expected_result: Each added country turns teal and the total increments.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.09 - INSERT and ADD data - Travel Tracker Part 2/Travel Tracker/solution2.js

pitfalls: Column list and value list in a different order or of a different length.
Forgetting single quotes around string literals.
Not excluding the id when the CSV has none, or excluding it when the CSV (countries.csv) does have one.
Inserting a duplicate country violates UNIQUE and throws, which is unhandled here.
No response when the name is not found.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'INSERT and parameterised queries': blurb on adding data safely from a form.
Tasks: write an INSERT, convert hard-coded values to $1/$2 placeholders, look up a code by name, redirect after insert.
Starter idea: in-memory fake db.query that logs the SQL text and values array.
Interactive demo: show text and values side by side, and an injection attempt contrasted between concatenated and parameterised queries.
